title: Quantum Mechanics I
source_note: This is the Mathematics department's own mathematical-methods treatment of introductory quantum mechanics (standard NUC-aligned 400L content), emphasising the operator/wavefunction formalism: the Schrodinger equation, wavefunctions and the Born interpretation, position/momentum/Hamiltonian operators, commutators and Hermitian operators, the uncertainty principle, and the exactly solvable problems (infinite square well, harmonic oscillator, tunneling).

questions.question: The time-dependent Schrodinger equation for a particle of mass m in potential V(x,t) is:
options: i hbar dPsi/dt = -(hbar^2/2m) d^2 Psi/dx^2 + V Psi
questions.correct_answer: i hbar dPsi/dt = -(hbar^2/2m) d^2 Psi/dx^2 + V Psi
questions.explanation: This is the fundamental equation governing the time evolution of a quantum wavefunction in one spatial dimension.

questions.question: The time-independent Schrodinger equation is obtained from the time-dependent one, for a time-independent potential, by separating variables as:
questions.explanation: This separation of variables produces stationary states with definite energy E, reducing the PDE to an ODE for psi(x).

questions.question: According to the Born interpretation, |Psi(x,t)|^2 represents:
options: The probability density of finding the particle at position x at time t
questions.correct_answer: The probability density of finding the particle at position x at time t
questions.explanation: The Born rule gives physical meaning to the wavefunction as a probability amplitude whose modulus squared is a probability density.

questions.question: For a wavefunction to be physically acceptable, it must be normalized so that:
options: The integral over all space of |Psi(x,t)|^2 dx equals 1
The integral of Psi dx equals 0
questions.correct_answer: The integral over all space of |Psi(x,t)|^2 dx equals 1
questions.explanation: Normalization ensures the total probability of finding the particle somewhere in space is exactly one.

questions.question: In quantum mechanics, the position operator acts on a wavefunction by:
questions.explanation: In the position representation, the position operator simply multiplies the wavefunction by x.

questions.question: The momentum operator in the position representation is given by:
questions.explanation: This differential operator representation of momentum is essential to the mathematical formalism of quantum mechanics.

questions.question: The Hamiltonian operator H-hat for a particle in one dimension is:
questions.explanation: The Hamiltonian operator represents the total energy, combining the kinetic energy operator with the potential energy function.

questions.question: The commutator of two operators A-hat and B-hat is defined as:
questions.explanation: The commutator measures the failure of two operators to commute and is central to quantum mechanical structure.

questions.question: The canonical commutation relation between position and momentum operators is:
questions.explanation: This fundamental commutation relation encodes the impossibility of simultaneously specifying exact position and momentum.

questions.question: An operator A-hat is Hermitian if it satisfies:
options: The inner product <psi|A-hat phi> equals <A-hat psi|phi> for all suitable psi, phi
questions.correct_answer: The inner product <psi|A-hat phi> equals <A-hat psi|phi> for all suitable psi, phi
questions.explanation: This self-adjointness condition is the defining property of a Hermitian operator.

questions.question: Physical observables in quantum mechanics are represented by operators that are:
questions.explanation: Since measurement outcomes must be real numbers, observables are represented by Hermitian operators.

questions.question: Eigenfunctions of a Hermitian operator corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are:
questions.explanation: This orthogonality is a general theorem for Hermitian operators and underlies the expansion of states in an eigenbasis.

questions.question: The expectation value of an observable A-hat in a normalized state Psi is computed as:
options: The integral of Psi* A-hat Psi dx
questions.correct_answer: The integral of Psi* A-hat Psi dx
questions.explanation: This sandwich integral gives the average value that would be obtained from many measurements of the observable on identically prepared systems.

questions.question: The Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle for position and momentum states that:
options: Delta x times Delta p is greater than or equal to hbar/2
Delta x times Delta p equals 0
Delta x equals Delta p always
Delta x times Delta p is less than or equal to hbar/2
questions.correct_answer: Delta x times Delta p is greater than or equal to hbar/2
questions.explanation: This inequality places a fundamental lower bound on the product of the uncertainties in position and momentum.

questions.question: The uncertainty principle arises mathematically from the fact that position and momentum operators:
questions.explanation: The general uncertainty relation for two observables is proportional to the expectation value of their commutator, which is nonzero for x and p.

questions.question: For a particle in an infinite square well of width L (from 0 to L), the allowed energy levels are:
questions.explanation: Solving the time-independent Schrodinger equation with infinite walls at 0 and L gives quantized energies proportional to n squared.

questions.question: The ground state wavefunction of the infinite square well (from 0 to L) is:
options: psi_1(x) = square root of (2/L) times sin(pi x/L)
psi_1(x) = square root of (2/L) times cos(pi x/L)
questions.correct_answer: psi_1(x) = square root of (2/L) times sin(pi x/L)
questions.explanation: This is the normalized lowest-energy eigenfunction, vanishing at both walls as required by the boundary conditions.

questions.question: In the infinite square well, the wavefunction must vanish at the walls because:
options: The potential is infinite outside the well, so the wavefunction must be continuous and zero there
The particle cannot have zero energy
The wavefunction is always zero everywhere
questions.correct_answer: The potential is infinite outside the well, so the wavefunction must be continuous and zero there
questions.explanation: Continuity of the wavefunction, combined with it being zero outside the infinite barrier, forces it to vanish exactly at the walls.

questions.question: The energy levels of the quantum harmonic oscillator are given by:
options: E_n = hbar omega/2 for all n
questions.explanation: The harmonic oscillator has evenly spaced energy levels shifted up from zero by the zero-point energy hbar omega/2.

questions.question: The nonzero ground-state energy of the quantum harmonic oscillator (E_0 = hbar omega/2) is a direct consequence of:
questions.explanation: A particle cannot have both zero position uncertainty and zero momentum uncertainty at the bottom of the well, forcing a minimum nonzero energy.

questions.question: The raising and lowering (ladder) operators a-dagger and a for the harmonic oscillator satisfy the commutation relation:
questions.explanation: This canonical commutation relation between the ladder operators underlies the algebraic solution of the harmonic oscillator.

questions.question: The eigenfunctions of the quantum harmonic oscillator are expressed in terms of:
options: Hermite polynomials multiplied by a Gaussian
questions.correct_answer: Hermite polynomials multiplied by a Gaussian
questions.explanation: Solving the harmonic oscillator's Schrodinger equation produces Hermite polynomials modulated by a Gaussian envelope.

questions.question: In the quantum tunneling problem, a particle with energy E less than a potential barrier height V0 has a wavefunction inside the barrier that:
options: Decays exponentially but is nonzero, giving a nonzero probability of transmission
Oscillates freely as if there were no barrier
questions.correct_answer: Decays exponentially but is nonzero, giving a nonzero probability of transmission
questions.explanation: The exponentially decaying solution inside a classically forbidden region does not vanish entirely, allowing tunneling through thin barriers.

questions.question: Classically, a particle with E less than V0 could never cross a potential barrier; quantum mechanically, tunneling is possible because:
options: The wavefunction does not vanish abruptly at the barrier, allowing a nonzero amplitude to persist on the far side
The Schrodinger equation does not apply to barriers
questions.correct_answer: The wavefunction does not vanish abruptly at the barrier, allowing a nonzero amplitude to persist on the far side
questions.explanation: Wavefunction continuity across the barrier allows a small but nonzero transmitted amplitude beyond the barrier.

questions.question: For a step potential where E is greater than V0, the wave is partially reflected and partially transmitted at the step; this is analogous to:
options: Partial reflection of light at a change in refractive index
questions.correct_answer: Partial reflection of light at a change in refractive index
questions.explanation: Just as light partially reflects at an interface between media, a matter wave partially reflects at a potential step even when it has enough energy to pass.

questions.question: The probability current (flux) density j(x,t) is constructed so that it satisfies a continuity equation with the probability density, expressing:
questions.explanation: The continuity equation for the probability density and current ensures total probability is conserved over time, consistent with unitary evolution.

questions.question: Stationary states of the time-independent Schrodinger equation have wavefunctions whose overall time dependence e^(-iEt/hbar) means that:
questions.explanation: Since the time factor has unit modulus, it cancels in |Psi|^2, so probability densities of stationary states are time-independent.

questions.question: The superposition principle in quantum mechanics states that if Psi1 and Psi2 are both solutions of the Schrodinger equation, then:
options: Any linear combination c1 Psi1 + c2 Psi2 is also a solution
Psi1 times Psi2 is a solution
questions.correct_answer: Any linear combination c1 Psi1 + c2 Psi2 is also a solution
questions.explanation: The Schrodinger equation is linear, so any superposition of its solutions is itself a valid solution.

questions.question: Any two eigenfunctions of the Hamiltonian corresponding to different energy eigenvalues are automatically:
questions.explanation: Since the Hamiltonian is Hermitian, its eigenfunctions with distinct eigenvalues are guaranteed to be orthogonal.

questions.question: The de Broglie relation connecting a particle's momentum p to its associated wavelength lambda is:
questions.explanation: This relation, proposed by de Broglie, extends wave-particle duality from photons to all matter.

questions.question: The expectation value of momentum for a real-valued, normalizable bound-state wavefunction, such as an infinite-well eigenstate, is:
questions.explanation: For a real stationary-state wavefunction the momentum expectation value vanishes, reflecting that the particle is equally likely to be moving in either direction.

questions.question: Degenerate energy levels in quantum mechanics refer to a situation where:
options: More than one linearly independent eigenfunction corresponds to the same energy eigenvalue
The system has no bound states
questions.correct_answer: More than one linearly independent eigenfunction corresponds to the same energy eigenvalue
questions.explanation: Degeneracy occurs when a single energy value admits multiple distinct quantum states, common in systems with symmetry.
